These results demonstrate that gradient-estimator design expands the capabilities of neural-network variational methods for accurate scientific computing.

articles.title: Factors Influencing Radio Frequency Disinfestation of Dried Figs Based on Dielectric Properties and Heat Tolerance
articles.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) disinfestation, owing to its efficient and selective heating, is a promising method for controlling pests in stored dried figs. This study investigated the dielectric properties of dried figs and the Indianmeal moths (Plodia interpunctella) and evaluated the thermal tolerance of the Indianmeal moth during RF treatment. Dried figs with moisture contents of 12%, 16%, and 20% and the Indianmeal moths at the egg, young-larval, and late-instar stages were examined. The effects of frequency, temperature, and moisture content on fig dielectric properties were determined; the dielectric responses of 20%-moisture figs and insects were compared; and stage-specific insect heating rates were measured. Mortality was assessed under RF heating with hot-air holding at 45, 48, 51, and 54 °C with holding times of 2, 4, 8, and 12 min. Across 10–3000 MHz, the dielectric constant and loss factor of dried figs showed frequency-dependent trends, generally decreasing with frequency but increasing with temperature and moisture content. At 20% moisture, both parameters were significantly lower in figs than in the Indianmeal moths at 20–80 °C, with the disparity increasing at higher temperatures. At 50 °C, 27.12 MHz showed the largest loss-factor contrast (209.04) between dried figs and late-instar Indianmeal moth larvae, indicating the greatest selective RF heating potential. Early-instar larvae heated fastest, at 4.01 °C min⁻¹, whereas late-instar larvae exhibited the greatest heat tolerance. Mortality increased significantly with temperature and holding time. These findings provide a basis for safe, efficient, and environmentally friendly RF disinfestation of dried figs.

articles.title: Mapping the genetic links of broad cognition and language to brain structure: A two-factor Genomic SEM analysis
articles.abstract: Cognitive abilities share substantial genetic architecture, but it is unclear whether their genetic relationships with brain structure primarily reflect broad cognitive variation or domain-related components such as language. We used linkage disequilibrium score regression and Genomic Structural Equation Modeling to model correlated broad-cognition and language factors from 12 published cognitive GWAS. We first tested a frozen UK Biobank atlas of 114 imaging-derived phenotypes (66 hemisphere-specific cortical surface-area measures and 48 white-matter fractional-anisotropy measures), then prospectively triangulated the cortical results in 34 bilateral ENIGMA-3 surface-area GWAS. In UK Biobank, no direct cognition-versus-language brain covariance contrast survived within-family FDR correction, although broad cognition showed 12 cortical and 11 white-matter factor-specific FDR associations versus 2 cortical and 0 white-matter associations for language. In ENIGMA, 33/34 broad-cognition and 16/34 language associations survived the prespecified 68-test FDR. Two direct cortical contrasts survived the 34-region FDR: superior parietal cortex (cognition r_g = 0.197; language r_g=-0.012; P = 9.0×10⁻⁵; q = 0.0031) and precuneus (cognition r_g = 0.251; language r_g = 0.074; P = 0.00185; q = 0.0315); superior parietal cortex also survived Bonferroni correction. Across 33 cortical regions shared by UK Biobank and ENIGMA, regional maps correlated r = 0.719 for cognition and r = 0.781 for language. Fixing the small Spelling residual variance to zero preserved every multiple-testing decision. Broad cognition therefore shows a highly distributed structural-brain genetic architecture, language a more selective pattern, and specific parietal regions show corrected evidence of stronger genetic coupling to broad cognition than to language.

articles.title: Explainable Multi-Agent Financial Advisory: Design and Comparative Evaluation of Collaborative Reasoning Models for Investment Recommendation
articles.abstract: Generative-AI agents are increasingly proposed for investment analysis, yet two questions remain under-examined: how should multiple specialist agents combine their opinions, and what does the combination cost in explainability? This paper designs a ﬁnancial multi-agent advisory framework in which four tool-grounded analyst agents—momentum, mean-reversion, risk, and macro-regime—emit bounded conviction scores, conﬁdences, and structured evidence. On top of a single agent interface we formalize six collaborative reasoning models as coalition-evaluable operators: a best single agent, uniform voting, conﬁdence-weighted fusion, iterative debate (DeGroot-style consensus formation), a hierarchical coordinator with risk-veto authority, and a learned ridge-regression fusion. Coali-tion evaluability makes exact Shapley attributions over agents computable in closed form (24 coalitions), yielding a uniﬁed explanation object—per-agent attributions, evidence rationale, disagreement-based uncertainty, and a natural-language brief—for every recommendation, regardless of the reasoning model. In a 4.6-year out-of-sample evaluation (2022–2026) on ten large-cap U.S. equities with transaction costs, conﬁdence-weighted fusion and debate achieve Sharpe ratios of 1.03 and 1.02 versus 0.78 for a passive S&P 500 benchmark and 0.74 for the best single agent, while the hierarchical veto committee is over-conservative (0.52); block bootstrap shows this protocol ordering is robust (stable in 99.7% of resamples) even where absolute market outperformance is not statistically separable at this horizon. Explanation faithfulness degrades monotonically with reasoning interactivity (from 1.00 for additive committees to 0.78 for debate) even though exact Shapley attributions remain stable under input perturbation (≥0.995 cosine similarity), quantifying an explainability cost of collaboration that simple deletion-based explanations would misreport. All data, code, ﬁgures, and tables are reproducible from a released Python artifact.

articles.title: Flexible Data Access Mechanisms for IoT Ecosystems: From Content-Based Addressing to LLM-Driven Data Acquisition
articles.abstract: The continuous development and integration of public and private Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures require flexible and scalable data access mechanisms that ensure seamless access to IoT data regardless of its source of physical address. Traditionally, retrieving data from different physical sources requires rigid, topology-dependent protocols and high technical skills; this may limit accessibility for a wider range of end-users.Content-Based Addressing (CBA) accesses data based on its attributes or content rather than its network location. Users need an intuitive mechanism to extract IoT values from multiple sources (e.g. public and private sources), removing the need for technical database query knowledge. In a similar way to web search (e.g. Google), users ask questions in natural language based on content, location and time without direct reference to the physical location of the IoT devices that provide the necessary information. This paper proposes a novel, hybrid framework for flexible IoT data access that combines CBA with a Large Language Model (LLM)-based conversational interface. The architecture is built on two core pillars: a Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) layer, coupled with a device registry, that unifies heterogeneous data sources, public APIs and private edge devices, into a single content-addressed store secured by a granular Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) mechanism. The second pillar is a Natural Language Query Engine that translates chat-based interrogations into executable system queries.An adaptive imputation service maintains data completeness by detecting missing sensor readings, predicting replacement values, and reconciling predictions when delayed measurements arrive. Together, the framework enables an intuitive experience for IoT data exploration with no technical training needed.

articles.title: BirdNova: A Web-Based Bird Species Identification Platform Using Separate Image and Audio Deep Learning Models
articles.abstract: Bird species identification supports biodiversity research and wildlife monitoring, but manual identification can be difficult when species have similar visual characteristics or vocalisations. This paper presents BirdNova, a web-based application that provides bird identification through two independent deep-learning workflows: image classification and audio classification. The image workflow resizes input photographs to 224 × 224 pixels and processes them using a convolutional neural network (CNN). The audio workflow converts recordings to mono audio at 22,050 Hz, standardises their duration to five seconds by trimming or padding, and generates Mel-spectrogram representations for a separate audio classifier. The two models are accessed through a common Flask-based interface but do not perform feature-level or decision-level fusion. The image classifier was evaluated on an independent test set of 1,753 images covering 25 bird species. It achieved 80.03% test accuracy, 81.49% weighted precision, 80.03% weighted recall, and 79.93% weighted F1-score. Validation accuracy was 95.96%, a difference of 15.93 percentage points from independent test accuracy. This gap indicates that generalisation requires further investigation. The current manuscript documents the audio workflow but does not report a complete quantitative evaluation of that module; therefore, no audio performance claim is made. BirdNova is presented as an application-level integration of separate image and audio classifiers, with its evaluation limitations explicitly identified.

articles.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
articles.abstract: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

articles.title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
articles.abstract: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

articles.title: Efficient interlayer interactions in non-planar molecule/transition-metal dichalcogenide two-dimensional heterostructure
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integration of molecules and two-dimensional (2D) atomic materials offer new opportunities for hybrid electronic devices. Most progress has focused on interfacing planar molecule. In contrast, incorporating non-planar molecules into 2D heterostructures remains challenging due to the three-dimensional orientations of ligands. Here we investigate interlayer interactions between discrete non-planar spin-crossover (SCO) molecules, [Fe(tBu2qsal)2] (FTBQS), monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) spacers through optical spectroscopies. FTBQS features bulk molecular crystal layers and can be mechanically exfoliated, enabling deterministic assembly of clean hybrid heterostructures. Robust photoluminescence (PL) quenching, even with an hBN spacer, indicates efficient Förster resonance energy transfer with a long decay distance. Gate-dependent optical spectroscopy further identifies charge transfer from the doping shifts in the TMD layers due to the TMD/FTBQS electronic band alignment. Our results establish efficient interlayer interactions between non-plana, discrete molecules and 2D crystals for hybrid electrical, optical, and spintronic devices.

articles.title: Predicting solid-state reaction onset temperatures from high-throughput pairwise synthesis
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solid-state synthesis still relies on heuristics to choose reaction temperatures. The most widely used, Tammann's rule, places reaction onset at two-thirds of the lowest precursor melting point, but has never been systematically tested. Using an automated laboratory, we heated 1,035 pairwise combinations of 46 common precursors at their Tammann temperatures and identified the products by x-ray diffraction. Only 25% of pairs formed products containing both precursors. Combining these outcomes with text-mined literature syntheses, we trained log-normal accelerated failure time models that treat each fixed-temperature experiment as a bound on the unknown onset temperature. On 26 reactions with onset temperatures measured by in situ x-ray diffraction, a three-descriptor model reduced the mean absolute error from 131degC (Tammann's rule) to 88degC; adding 29 further physicochemical descriptors did not improve the model. Reaction onset can therefore be predicted from routine pass/fail synthesis outcomes, and predictions will improve as such data accumulates.

articles.title: Layer-dependent s± superconducting pairing and influence of incipient bands in La₃Ni₂O₇ thin films on real LaSrAlO₄ substrate
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by recent advances in ambient-pressure superconducting La₃Ni₂O₇ (LNO) thin films, we theoretically investigate these films by explicitly incorporating the realistic LaSrAlO₄ (LSAO) substrate. The Fermi-surface topology of the nickelate thin film closely resembles that of the high-pressure bulk phase, with similar α and β sheets and a small hole-like γ pocket originating from the surface bilayer (BL3). The bonding d₃z^₂₋ᵣ^₂ state of the interfacial bilayer (BL1, adjacent to the LSAO substrate) lies only sim 5 meV below the Fermi level, giving rise to an incipient γ band, while for the middle bilayer (BL2) its energy is much lower (sim 95 meV). Remarkably, no significant spontaneous charge transfer from the LSAO substrate to the LNO film is found. Instead, {it symmetry-allowed charge disproportionation} occurs between the BLs, with hole doping in BL3 and electron doping in BL1 and BL2. Via the weak-coupling Random Phase Approximation, we find a strong s±-wave superconducting pairing instability in BL3, while dₓ^₂₋y^₂ and s± are nearly degenerate in the other bilayers BL1 and BL2. Including the incipient γ band via the Dynamical Cluster Approximation beyond weak coupling, robust s±-wave pairing is observed in all three layers

articles.title: Fast closed-loop STEM navigation using vision-language models with typed decisions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closed-loop scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), in which each acquired image determines the next field of view and magnification, offers a route to autonomous atomic-scale materials analysis. Such a loop would automate navigation to defects and grain boundaries, a task that has long relied on operator judgment, and would enable systematic analysis of diverse local structures at scale. Realizing it hinges on the decision step, which must translate each acquired image into the next operation both quickly and correctly; yet which decision method can deliver both remains unclear. Here, we isolate this decision step. Using simulated atomic-resolution STEM images of a substitutional W dopant and a grain boundary in monolayer MoS₂, where the true target position is known and every method starts from identical conditions, we compared four vision-language models (VLMs) and three decision methods. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of Typed Decision, which directly obtains the probabilities of candidate labels from a pretrained VLM, for closed-loop STEM navigation. Typed Decision showed the shortest decision latency for all models (0.13-0.21 s) and generally achieved the highest navigation success rate among the three methods: it was the best for all models in W dopant navigation (66-91%) and for the best-performing model, Cosmos-Reason2 32B, in grain boundary navigation (43%). Furthermore, navigation to the different targets, the W dopant and the grain boundary, was possible by natural-language specification alone, without task-specific training of the VLM. These results indicate that Typed Decision is an effective decision method for realizing fast, accurate, and flexible closed-loop STEM.

articles.title: Interface Weyl electrons in the kagome-bilayers
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What makes a topological character prominent is whether its characteristic electronic states are located near the Fermi energy. While the kagome-metals possess unique topological characteristics owing to their distinctive electronic band structures, i.e. flat and Dirac bands, the control of Fermi energy to accentuate these characteristics has scarcely been studied in these materials. Here, we propose a new concept for activating the topological characteristics of Weyl electrons specifically near the interface of kagome-bilayers, namely interface Weyl electrons. The kagome-bilayers prepared by a sputtering technique surprisingly exhibit atomically abrupt interfaces thanks to the suppression of interdiffusion for maintaining the crystal symmetry of the hexagonal-type D0₁₉ and cubic-type L1₂ structures. Much higher electrical conductivity of the kagome-bilayers compared to single-layer films indicates the emergent contribution of a highly conductive electronic state at the interfaces. The enhanced electrical conductivity and the exceptionally large anomalous Hall conductivity about 2000 Ω⁻¹cm⁻¹ in the intrinsic mechanism indicates that the emergent interface electronic states comprise Weyl nodes in the D0₁₉ structure identified in our theoretical band calculations, triggered by nontrivial charge transfer. These results demonstrate that topological transport can be engineered at the interface of intermetallic compounds, leading further design principles towards development of device functionality.

articles.title: Implementation of LDA+Gutzwiller with Newton's method
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In order to calculate the electronic structure of correlated materials, we propose implementation of the LDA+Gutzwiller method with Newton's method. The self-consistence process, efficiency and convergence of calculation are improved dramatically by using Newton's method with golden section search and other improvement approaches. We compare the calculated results by applying the previous linear mix method and Newton's method. We have applied our code to study the electronic structure of several typical strong correlated materials, including SrVO₃, LaCoO₃, and La₂O₃Fe₂Se₂. Our results fit quite well with the previous studies.

articles.title: Molecular Kondo Ball Based on an Endohedral Fullerene
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically predict a molecular Kondo ball in TiSc₂N@C₈₀/Al(111), where a Ti-centered S = 1/2 local moment is encapsulated within a closed fullerene π cage that serves as an itinerant-like electronic reservoir for Kondo screening. First-principles calculations show that intermediate molecule--substrate hybridization broadens the discrete C₈₀ molecular levels into itinerant-like electronic states while preserving the Ti local moment, with similar electronic conditions found for Cd(0001) and In(101).Hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) simulations reveal a temperature-dependent Fano resonance with a Kondo temperature of about 60 K.The key electronic characteristics underlying the Kondo state remain robust against adsorption orientation, demonstrating that the closed cage geometry provides an orientation-tolerant molecular architecture for Kondo screening.

articles.title: Reconciling Models for Infinite-Layer Nickelate Superconductors: Role of Interstitial-s Band or A-Pocket
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding the minimal model that captures the essential physics of infinite-layer nickelate superconductors remains a central challenge. Using first-principles density-functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT), we compute and compare the strongly correlated electronic structures and optical spectra of various effective models for the infinite-layer nickelate LaNiO₂, ranging from a dₓ^₂₋y^₂ 1-band model to a full 6-band model with all Ni-3d plus an interstitial-s orbital. The results demonstrate that Ni-3d 5-band models overestimate the Hundness picture, whereas 6-band models, which explicitly include the interstitial-s band and have an A-pocket, recover the characteristic Mottness physics. Importantly, the influence of the interstitial-s band on the correlations of the dₓ^₂₋y^₂ band is negligible. Thus, superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates can be reliably described within a single-band Hubbard framework, while the accurate description of inter-orbital properties such as (optical) conductivities requires the inclusion of at least the interstitial-s band.

articles.title: Curvature Gradients Turn Shear into Superflow in Supersolids
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Supersolids on curved surfaces are becoming experimentally accessible. We develop a Galilean-covariant effective field theory of supersolids on curved surfaces and show that gradients of Gaussian curvature couple lattice shear to compression with a strength fixed by the shear modulus and the curvature gradient. As a result, shear drives superflow. On spheroids this yields geometric selection rules and multiplet splittings; near mode crossings, weak deformations produce hybrids in which superfluid and lattice carry comparable kinetic energy, and shear becomes visible as a density response.

articles.title: Spontaneous emission of atomic systems near metallic and semiconducting atomic chains
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the spontaneous emission of a quantum emitter placed near finite atomic chains described by the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By tuning the chain from a metallic to a semiconducting character through dimerization, we analyze how the electronic structure of an atomic-scale scatterer, together with the illumination profile, determines the strength, bandwidth, and spatial structure of the spontaneous emission enhancement. The resonant enhancement depends on both spectral matching and the emitter position relative to the induced charge and field patterns. In metallic chains, the nearly harmonic energy spectrum leads to overlapping optical transitions and strong resonances. For semiconducting chains, dimerization opens a gap and leads to a modified density of electronic states, redistributing the response over a broader spectral range and reducing its peak intensity. Coulomb interactions affect the optical resonances through blueshift or modification of their spatial character, and act differently on collective and single-particle-like excitations. Finally, we show that the same mechanisms demonstrated in atomic chains persist in realistic quasi-one-dimensional systems, including trans-polyacetylene chains and graphene nanoribbons. Our findings indicate a general direction for engineering light-matter interactions at the atomic scale, and may offer design principles for tunable nanoscale photonic and quantum-optical devices.

articles.title: Numerical integration of non-local master equations for renewal shot noise with drift and state-dependent amplitude
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The probability density of a system driven by a drift and a renewal train of kicks with state-dependent amplitude obeys a master equation that is non-local in space, because the kick operator hatp(ipartialₓ I(x)) is of infinite order, and, for non-exponential waiting times, non-local in time, with a memory kernel containing the propagator of the drift. Its solutions contain quasi-singular components, the never-kicked mass, which collapse onto the attractors of the drift. We present an accurate numerical method for such equations. The kick operator is a push-forward along the Marcus flow; in the Lamperti variable it becomes a translation, whose exact cell-to-cell weights follow from the cumulative distribution of the kicks, without quadrature. The drift is integrated by a conservative semi-Lagrangian step exact in time. The memory is represented by a sum of exponentials whose auxiliary fields are advected by the drift, at a cost linear in the number of steps. The never-kicked mass is transported exactly. For each ingredient we quantify the errors of simpler alternatives. The method is verified against exact solutions and event-driven Monte Carlo simulations with exact flow maps, from which it is statistically indistinguishable with 10⁸ trajectories. Parameters tuned for Gaussian kicks carry over unchanged to other kick distributions, and near a zero of the coupling, where the density vanishes faster than any power, the solution follows the known asymptotic law down to densities of order 10⁻³⁷, far beyond Monte Carlo reach. As an application we compare the exact equation with its local and Poissonian approximations: in the range explored, the local equation deviates by up to 8% of the density width, also for waiting times with finite mean, consistently with an error estimate predicting larger deviations for slow drifts at long times. A Fortran implementation is available.

articles.title: A Monte Carlo study of closely packed two-patch particles with frustrated interactions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently it was found that closely packed two-patch particles exhibit rich orientational ordering behaviors, e.g., nonmonotonic changes of the nematic order parameter and double BKT phase transitions [arXiv:2509.03981]. In this work, we show that, with repulsive patch-patch, attractive patch-nonpatch and intermediate nonpatch-nonpatch interactions, there exist frustrations in the system of closely packed two-patch particles. To investigate the ground states of the system, we design a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm with single-defect propagation. The simulation results show that the ground states are disordered and the correlation functions decay exponentially with the distance. These results demonstrate that in 2D close packing one could design patchy particles to explore orientationally disordered systems.

articles.title: Finite-temperature effects on the single-particle Green's function of a mobile impurity in a Luttinger liquid
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of a quadratically-dispersing quantum impurity interacting through a contact density-density term with a one-dimensional (1D) superfluid described by Luttinger liquid theory. By means of a field-theoretical approach based on the linked-cluster expansion, we quantitatively address the effects of a finite temperature of the 1D bath on the momentum-space single-particle Green's function. Through a careful identification of the resonant phonon-impurity scattering processes, we obtain asymptotic large-time estimates for the thermally-induced exponential damping of the zero-temperature signal both in the quasiparticle regime, dominated by the presence of a finite lifetime for the host impurity, and in the infrared-dominated regime, where the impurity causes a Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe of the 1D bath. In both cases, we identify a temperature-induced coherence time that sets the characteristic timescale of the exponentially-decaying finite-temperature correction to the amplitude of the zero-temperature single-particle Green's function. Moreover, we draw connections between the aforesaid thermal timescale and the microscopic parameters of the Lieb-Liniger model, which admits an effective Luttinger-liquid description, highlighting the dependence of the inverse coherence time on the intra-bath interactions across the different dynamical regimes of the impurity.

articles.title: Zero-Temperature Energetics of a First-Order Surface Phase Transition from Diffraction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: First-order phase transitions are governed by the balance between zero-temperature energy, thermal vibrational energy, and entropy, yet these contributions are rarely accessible experimentally. Here, we establish a diffraction-based route to determine them for the prototypical Si(111)-In atomic-wire system. From the temperature-dependent Debye-Waller attenuation of reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) intensities we extract distinct Debye temperatures for the low-temperature (8×2) ground state and the high-temperature (4×1) phase. The softer vibrational spectrum of the high-temperature phase yields the entropy gain that stabilizes this phase above the critical temperature T_c. Evaluating the thermodynamic balance between internal energy and entropy at T_c = 125,K yields a zero-temperature energy difference of Δ E₀ = 138,meV/(8×2), including the difference in vibrational zero-point energies of the two phases, thus providing direct access to hidden thermodynamic parameters of a first-order surface phase transition.

articles.title: Computing with Orientation-Dependent Vector Fields in Crystallographic Texture Analysis
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a computational framework for representing orientation-dependent vector fields. Building on (arXiv:2608.21235), we translate the differential-geometric formulation into crystallographic notation and focus on its computational use in crystallographic texture analysis. In crystallographic applications, small orientation changes are commonly described by rotation vectors, spin tensors, or infinitesimal misorientations. By contrast, vector fields in harmonic computations are usually represented by components with respect to Euler-angle derivatives, following the classical formulation of generalized spherical harmonics. This representation is convenient but numerically unfavorable. We instead use rotation-vector components, extending a familiar description of individual orientation changes to orientation-dependent vector fields. In this representation, vector fields are described by three scalar component functions, which can be expanded into generalized spherical harmonics. We derive frequency-domain formulas for gradient, divergence, and curl, enabling their evaluation directly on harmonic coefficients. In particular, the gradient of a band-limited scalar function remains band-limited with the same bandwidth.

articles.title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23375v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

articles.title: Symmetry classification of hyperfine rovibrational molecular phase space
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symmetry-based structures have advanced molecular spectroscopy and quantum information science, yet connections between these fields remain largely unexplored. We construct a phase space theory of a molecule by jointly treating rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin degrees of freedom as the quotient of orientations and normal coordinates by the molecule's point group. The various combinations of how these three degrees of freedom transform under symmetries organize a molecule's states into molecular species, and we show that each species is defined by a particular absolutely maximally entangled (AME) carrier state, or, for 45 species, by a two-dimensional space of them. Up to local unitaries and the order of the sectors, molecular species realize 21 AME states across 75 point groups: a product state, four maximally entangled pairs, and 16 genuinely tripartite states. A Fourier transform on the quotient relates orientation and angular-momentum descriptions while preserving these carrier states. We propose an example experimental protocol for preparing and driving symmetry-adapted bend states of CaOCH₃.

articles.title: Real-space electrostatic sums through truncation error analysis
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23510v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Methods that treat electrostatics in real space, without explicit reciprocal-space evaluation, are appealing for large-scale atomistic simulations. They typically employ local charge-neutralization schemes, but their relationship to the underlying error contributions of the full Ewald sum has not been fully characterized. A principled basis for parameter selection is also lacking. In this work, we show that the correction terms of Wolf's and Pickard's real-space methods approximate the truncation error of real-space electrostatic sums. This perspective motivates simplified fixed-radii and force-shifted Pickard variants that preserve the truncation-error compensation behavior while enforcing continuity of pair energy and force at the cutoff. We derive a nonempirical scaling relation for the optimal path in the parameter space of the cutoff radius and screening distance, generalizing Pickard's empirical heuristic and explaining when and why it can fail. A systematic scheme for restoring omitted reciprocal contributions is introduced, which accelerates convergence to the full Ewald energy.

articles.title: Parisi Energy before Parisi Geometry in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23645v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The fractured low-energy landscape of spin glasses presents a notorious barrier to optimization. While high-depth calculations indicate that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can approach the Parisi ground-state energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, how it does so remains elusive. Here, we treat the QAOA distribution as a statistical-physics object and probe its geometry directly in the thermodynamic limit. We draw two independent bitstrings from the same problem instance and couple them through their macroscopic similarity. We find that typical QAOA samples remain macroscopically uncorrelated, even as their sensitivity to this coupling grows with circuit depth p. By contrast, the low-energy tail shows a much stronger tendency to overlap and reveals a Parisi-like phase with the same critical behavior as the thermal spin-glass transition. The onset of this organization moves toward the typical output as the circuit deepens, consistent with the separation vanishing only as p→infty. Together, these findings suggest a route distinct from structure-exploiting classical algorithms and thermal sampling, one in which the QAOA approaches the Parisi energy before Parisi geometry becomes typical.

articles.title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

articles.title: XANES-Guided Molecular Structure Generation via Conditional Diffusion and Forward Spectral Prediction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23725v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing complete molecular structures from X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra remains challenging because the spectra primarily encode local chemical environments, with overlapping contributions from multiple absorbing sites. Here, we develop an inverse-forward framework combining XANES-conditioned diffusion-based molecular structure generation with forward spectral prediction for candidate selection. The inverse model generates atomic species, bond connectivity, and three-dimensional coordinates from C, N, and O K-edge XANES, given only the total atom count without molecular formulas or element-specific atom counts. Combining all three absorption edges substantially improves structural recovery, achieving a best-of-10 exact-match rate of 56.6% across 2,888 test molecules. The generated candidates also reproduce functional groups and structural motifs, achieving a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.951 across 21 categories. Ranking candidates by agreement between input and forward-predicted spectra increases the exact-match rate from 24.3% for unranked top-1 selection to 43.9%. This spectral-consistency criterion also enables atom count estimation, identifying the correct count for 65.6% of molecules among seven tested values. Application to experimental spectra yields an exact structural match for imidazole and recovers characteristic functional groups in two additional molecules, while revealing limitations due to simulation-experiment spectral discrepancies. These findings establish an inverse-forward approach for reconstructing whole-molecule structures from complementary element-specific XANES information.

articles.title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23762v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances Ω_ϵ(N/log²N) and at least N¹⁻ϵ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed 0<ϵ<1. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to |0rangle, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent γ → 0 and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares N¹⁻ϵ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance Ω_ϵ(N/log²N). The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.

articles.title: A structure-based model of the bacterial chemosensory array reveals how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes sensory responses
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23921v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a structure-based Ising model of the bacterial chemosensory array to investigate how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes signaling responses. The model couples the activity states of core signaling units and of CheW subunits within hexameric rings on a lattice with the structure observed in cryoEM experiments. Recent experiments show that increasing CheW participation in hexameric rings raises response cooperativity in non-adapting cells and sensitivity in adaptation-proficient cells. Our lattice model quantitatively reproduces both effects, while mean-field theory shows that CheW increases the effective coupling between core units, sharpening the response in both cell types. The statistics of CheW placement (complete hexameric rings versus random distribution) substantially alter how responses vary with CheW abundance. Moreover, different coupling strengths can yield the same static response yet markedly different activity fluctuations and dynamics. CheW abundance further controls a crossover from relaxational to oscillatory fluctuations, whose location depends on the spatial distribution of CheW. These dynamical signatures, including oscillations predicted near native CheW levels, are testable by single-cell dynamics measurements. Combined with CheW titration and our modeling results, these measurements can probe the array's assembly dynamics and allosteric couplings. Beyond the chemosensory array, our approach can generalize to other large protein complexes, providing a framework to study the functional role of scaffolding proteins and allosteric interfaces in signal processing.

articles.title: Virtual Autopurification in Translationally Invariant Quantum States
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24448v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce virtual autopurification (VAP), a protocol for virtual purification that operates entirely within a single translationally invariant system. Virtual purification suppresses thermal fluctuations and decoherence noise by amplifying the dominant pure component of a mixed state, but its standard implementation requires multiple copies of the state and global entangled measurements. VAP avoids the multiple-copy overhead by constructing virtual copies from spatially separated subregions and performing entangled measurements only between them. Assuming clustering of correlations, we show that VAP reproduces the expectation values of the standard virtual purification protocol, with discrepancies that decay exponentially in both the buffer length and the inter-subregion distance. Numerical simulations support the theoretical predictions and demonstrate accurate implementation of virtual cooling with reduced resource requirements. Our results establish VAP as a resource-efficient and scalable approach to quantum-state purification in near-term devices.

articles.title: Mid-Infrared Integrated Acousto-Optic Phase Modulation on GaAs/AlGaAs
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24530v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We demonstrate a mid-infrared (7.5-10 um) integrated acousto-optic phase modulator operating at 460MHz based on a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure. The combination of broad mid-infrared transparency and piezoelectric properties of GaAs based structures allows monolithic integration of all the device functions (electro-acoustic transduction and acousto-optic interaction) on a single material platform. Addressing the challenge presented by comparable mid-infrared and acoustic wavelengths, simultaneous propagation and confinement of surface acoustic waves and guided light is achieved using a deep-etched sub-wavelength grating. We develop a comprehensive and quantitative simulation framework to design the modulator devices, characterize their acoustic properties in a heterodyne vibrometer and perform a full, quantitative analysis of the device performance by inserting them in an integrated Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Remarkable agreement with simulations validates the proposed design flow, and opens the way to improved integrated acousto-optic devices operating in the longer end of the mid-infrared.

articles.title: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC⁽¹⁾ in 1D
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. Even for first-order OTOCs, where growing evidence suggests classical tractability, no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has been established to date. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to 512 qubits for Clifford circuits with 768 T-gates and up to 22 qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.

articles.title: The magical memory cost of entanglement spectrum compression
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24710v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How much quantum memory is needed to faithfully retain the entanglement spectrum of a bipartite pure state after separating out Bell pairs through local unitaries? We derive the exact tradeoff between Bell-pair yield, residual memory, and reconstruction fidelity under local unitaries, defining an operational measure of entanglement-spectrum complexity. Smoothed entanglement spread bounds this memory cost from below, while diverging nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory at any fixed positive fidelity. Chaotic circuit dynamics exhibit a transient memory peak whose height increases with system size, followed by declining cost despite continued entropy growth. A large typical Haar-random state requires only an accuracy-dependent memory, whereas stationary fermionic Gaussian states retain a growing cost with size. In the circuits studied, the multiscale spectral structure associated with entanglement catalysis also has a practical consequence for matrix product state compression, yielding a multiplicative overhead not captured by the conventional entropy-based bond dimension estimate.

articles.title: An Atiyah--Hirzebruch to Adams map and the hastened Adams spectral sequence for supercohomology
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24725v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct a map of filtered spectra inducing a map from the Atiyah--Hirzebruch spectral sequence (AHSS) to the Baker--Lazarev Adams spectral sequence of a ko-module M. Using this and a theorem of Bruner--Rognes, we construct a hastened Adams spectral sequence (HASS) for the Postnikov truncations of ko and the connective Adams summand. Then, motivated by questions in quantum field theory, topological phases of matter, and tensor category theory, we apply the HASS to supercohomology, the cohomology theory IC^×(τₗₑ ₂ko), and observe that in examples of interest it is easier to calculate with than either the AHSS or the usual Adams spectral sequence. We include a User's Guide to the HASS and several worked examples, as well as hastened Adams charts for many commonly encountered A(1)-modules.

articles.title: 4D-TEMPO: Differentiable 4D-STEM ptychography via fast Physics Optimizers
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electron ptychography recovers atomic structure from 4D-STEM data: diffraction patterns at multiple positions of a scanned probe. Current codes reconstruct an image and read atoms off it, or fit atoms under an L₁ loss; neither gives per-atom uncertainty. We propose 4D-TEMPO, a differentiable physical renderer that fits the atoms, the microscope, and the detector directly to the recorded electron counts under a Poisson likelihood. The output is a list of atoms, each a Gaussian primitive with a 3D position, a thermal width, and a model-conditional error bar from the Fisher information. The Fisher information also conditions the solver, gives the dose (electrons per Å²) each parameter needs, and separates calibration from imaging. On a simulated WSe₂ bilayer, starting from the published reconstruction, fitted atoms cut in-plane error by a third (3.2 vs. 4.8 pm) and depth error by 40-61% against its 3D peaks. Depth comes from multiple scattering into the dark field, the faint counts outside the direct beam. The two layers, 10× closer than the depth of field, separate; per-atom depth then follows the layer geometry. When the model is well specified, the bars are calibrated (69% of position coordinates within 1σ). On experimental WSe₂, fitted atoms predict held-out patterns better than the three published codes we test. With free probe modes where atoms are incomplete, the same likelihood predicts best on all three held-out benchmarks, matches every WSe₂ baseline in 5 min against up to 20.5 h, and passes torchslice at its released setting 180× sooner on PrScO₃. Per-atom error bars, planned doses, and fast reconstruction point to low-dose, real-time 3D imaging of beam-sensitive and dynamic materials.

articles.title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24911v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform O(λ²) bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where λ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains O(λ²) accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.

articles.title: Hybrid metal-semiconductor quantum dots in InAs as a platform for quantum simulation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2508.03928v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Arrays of hybrid metal-semiconductor quantum dots offer a new approach to quantum simulation, with key advantages over arrays of conventional quantum dots. Because the metallic component of these hybrid dots has a quasi-continuous level spectrum, each site in an array can be effectively electronically identical; in contrast, each conventional semiconductor quantum dot has its own spectral fingerprint. Meanwhile, the semiconductor component retains gate-tunability of intersite coupling. This combination creates a scalable platform for simulating correlated ground states driven by Coulomb interactions. We report the fabrication and characterization of hybrid metal-semiconductor dots, featuring a submicron metal island transparently contacting a gate-confined region of an InAs quantum well with tunable couplings to macroscopic leads. Tuning the dot-lead coupling to the weak-coupling limit yields highly-uniform Coulomb peaks, with no resolvable excitation spectrum in the Coulomb diamonds. We propose a realistic device design for a hybrid dot-based linear array quantum simulator and outline the correlated many-body physics accessible in this architecture.

articles.title: GEODE: Symmetry-Preserving Cartesian Diffusion for Crystal Generation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.01898v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Most known inorganic crystals exhibit symmetric atomic arrangements, yet generative models often fail to reproduce them. Explicitly enforcing these symmetries has so far yielded fewer stable and novel structures than unconstrained generation. We introduce Generative Equivariant Orbit Diffusion Engine (GEODE), to our knowledge the first model to combine coordinate and lattice diffusion in Cartesian space. GEODE first samples symmetry templates, then jointly generates the lattice, atomic coordinates and atom types while preserving the specified symmetry with a novel Wyckoff-constrained loss. Cartesian diffusion gives coordinate noise a consistent physical scale that we empirically demonstrate improves performance. Unconditional generation achieves a metastable, unique and novel (mSUN) rate of 11.9%, compared with 7.7% for the next best symmetry-aware model. We also introduce sampling time template filtering, which increases mSUN by ~6% without retraining, making GEODE competitive with leading symmetry-agnostic models. Template selection also enables joint symmetry and property guidance, which we demonstrate through classifier-free guidance of permittivity.

articles.title: Thermodynamically Consistent Lindbladians for Quantum Stochastic Thermodynamics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2502.20118v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a thermodynamically consistent Lindblad approach for quantum stochastic thermodynamics, where each bath dissipator satisfies the local quantum detailed balance condition. We formulate the thermodynamic geometry to determine the optimal protocol in the slow-driving regime. Thermodynamic consistency leads to the joint fluctuation theorem for quantum work and heat, with the corresponding joint statistics obtained from a tilted master equation and generally described by a quasiprobability. We apply this framework to the quantum Brownian motion master equation, refining it to satisfy detailed balance, deriving optimal protocols at different temperatures and friction coefficients, and studying the work statistics. Our approach thus enables the study of nonequilibrium thermodynamics in open quantum systems.

articles.title: Quantum information spreading via higher-order operator correlators
articles.abstract: arXiv:2609.05472v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide an exact analytical benchmarks into measuring the quantum information spreading by introducing N-operator correlators. Leveraging the idea from N-point correlation function from cosmology, we formulate a generalized Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlator (OTOC), called N-Operator Correlator (NOC). Such formulation can reduce the effect of restricted analysis associated with selecting only two operators for OTOC. NOC can take into account a larger set of measurement probes in measuring the degree of quantum information spreading. We demonstrate these concepts with two analytically tractable systems with computing thermal averages of operator time evolutions at a finite temperature: a single qubit in longitudinal field and isotropic XXX model with a transverse field, two-qubit system. Our analytical benchmark serves as a basic introduction to generalized operator correlators in quantum mechanics.

articles.title: Bogoliubov self-consistent GW and second-order Green's function methods for attractive fermionic interactions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.03357v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Describing fermionic systems with attractive interactions, such as superconductors and atomic nuclei, beyond the mean-field level remains a central challenge. In this work, we investigate the performance of Bogoliubov fully self-consistent GW (Bog.~scGW) and second-order Green's function (Bog.~scGF2) methods, implemented within a unified imaginary-time and imaginary-frequency framework. Using two attractive Hubbard lattices (4×4 and 2×8) as a model study and benchmarking against full configuration interaction (FCI), we find that, for these systems, Bog.~scGF2 provides a more accurate description than Bog.~scGW. In particular, Bog.~scGW systematically overestimates the correlation energy, with errors increasing rapidly as the attractive interaction strength grows. These results suggest the importance of exchange contributions in such strongly correlated fermionic systems, even when exchange effects are included only at low order in perturbation theory.

articles.title: Graphene Transfer for Vertical Amorphous-Selenium Photodetectors: Fabrication, Optical Transmission and Operation at 77 K
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graphene can serve as a VUV transparent electrode in vertical photodetector devices. Using an optically transparent graphene as a top-electrode of amorphous selenium (a-Se) photoconductor requires transfer process compatible with the thermal and chemical sensitivities of a-Se thin films. The baking and polymer-removal steps of conventional commercial Trivial Transfer graphene procedures are undesirable because heating can promote selenium crystallization and prolonged solvent exposure can cause delamination. We implement two alternatives: PMMA-free transfer of nominal 50-layer graphene and transfer of nominal 10-layer graphene using an approximately 80 nm PMMA support removed in acetone at 40C. Raman G and 2D bands identify graphene after transfer. Separate graphene/MgF2 specimens are characterized by dark-corrected transmission measurements over 120-325 nm and compared with earlier single-layer and nominal 6-8-layer Trivial Transfer spectra. The completed graphene/a-Se/Cr devices produce bias-dependent voltage transients under pulsed 415 nm illumination at 293 K and 77 K. These results establish an a-Se-compatible fabrication route for graphene-electrode devices and demonstrate vertical device operation at both room and cryogenic temperatures. The completed devices provide a platform for detection-efficiency studies, and direct VUV photoresponse measurements now underway.

articles.title: Analysis of the Second-Harmonic Generation Process in Nonlinear Metasurfaces Based on Multiple Quantum Wells: The Approach of Nonlinear Current Density, and The Development of Boundary Conditions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using plasmonic metasurfaces integrated with nonlinear materials, such as multiple quantum wells (MQWs), has been an excellent solution to enhance nonlinear light-matter interactions. In this approach, a plasmonic resonator enhances the intensity of the fundamental harmonic within the MQWs region, increasing the strength of the intersubband transitions inside the MQWs. As a result, the efficiency of second harmonic generation (SHG) increases significantly. In this paper, we present a new approach to analyze the SHG process in nonlinear metasurfaces based on MQWs. In this approach, first, we formulate the nonlinear current density within the MQW region, which serves as the radiation source of the second harmonic wave. Notably, the saturation effect in MQWs, that limits the nonlinear response, is accounted for. Second, we address the development of boundary conditions for the second harmonic (SH) field in periodic structures, which ultimately leads us to define periodic boundary conditions for the SH field. Third, we combine these elements into a semi-analytical framework and validate it against previously reported experimental data. Finally, an efficient MQWs structure and plasmonic metasurface are designed for the fundamental wavelength of 8 μm. After implementing the proposed algorithm, we observe that the designed nonlinear metasurface achieves a significant conversion efficiency of 0.02% under the incident intensity of 23.5 kW/cm². KEYWORDS: Second harmonic generation, metasurface, multiple quantum wells, nonlinear current density, periodic boundary conditions

articles.title: Buoyancy-induced transitions in mixed convective flow past a heated square cylinder
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.23966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The effect of aiding buoyancy on flow past a square cylinder has previously been shown to suppress vortex shedding above a critical Richardson number (Ri), transitioning from unsteady to steady flow. Building on this, the present study uses two-dimensional direct numerical simulations (DNS) of vertically upward flow past a heated square cylinder to examine two buoyancy-induced transitions for a range of Ri and Reynolds number (Re). The secondary flow induced by buoyant force enhances positive entrainment in the momentum-deficit region aft of the cylinder, thereby suppressing vortex shedding. At higher Ri, this buoyant flow continues to gain downstream momentum, leading to a far-field plume-like instability. Extended domain simulations show that the far-field transition depends on the downstream distance available for buoyancy-driven disturbances to grow. Increasing Re delays near-field suppression but advances far-field instability. A local-flow analysis shows that a Reynolds number based on local mean velocity and plume width substantially improves the collapse of the far-field instability onset, while the corresponding plume-based Strouhal number also exhibits an approximate collapse across the investigated cases. Correlations for drag, surface-averaged Nusselt number, and far-field frequency are proposed using a mixed-convective velocity scale. Linear stability analysis (LSA) about the two-dimensional base flow captures both transitions as Hopf bifurcations and accurately predicts the dominant frequencies and finite-domain transition thresholds observed in DNS. The corresponding eigenmodes reveal localized oscillatory structures that shift downstream with increasing Ri. These results demonstrate the dual role of buoyancy in stabilizing the near wake while destabilizing the far field.

articles.title: Gas-induced reversible spectral tuning of bound states in the continuum in perovskite metasurfaces
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) provide a powerful route to engineering optical resonances in compact photonic structures, enabling enhanced light--matter interaction for sensing, nonlinear optics, optical modulation, and lasing. The next step towards practical BIC-based meta-optics is dynamic and reversible spectral control after fabrication. However, optical and electro-optical tuning typically produces limited refractive-index changes, thermo-optical approaches require continuous external actuation, and phase-change materials often provide discrete switching rather than continuous spectral reconfiguration. Here we demonstrate giant, fully reversible, and continuous spectral tuning of BIC resonances in halide-perovskite metasurfaces. Using nanoimprint lithography, we fabricate MAPbBr₃ metasurfaces, that support BIC-derived resonances in the visible spectral range. Exposure to HCl vapor initiates an anion-exchange reaction in which Cl⁻ ions diffuse into the perovskite crystalline lattice and partially replace Br⁻ ions, producing a monotonic increase of the electronic bandgap and blueshift of the excitonic resonance on a minute timescale. This leads to a decrease in the refractive index and tunes the BIC resonance by more than 40~nm in the visible range. Subsequent exposure to HBr vapor reverses the exchange process and restores the resonance to its initial spectral position. As a functional demonstration, we show continuous reversible spectral tuning of BIC-mediated lasing from the same metasurface. Our results establish gas-phase anion exchange as a non-destructive mechanism for continuous, reversible, and large-range post-fabrication control of perovskite metasurfaces, opening opportunities for chemically programmable lasers, adaptive meta-optics, and active nanophotonic devices.

articles.title: Probing the Nuclear E2 Transition Amplitude in ²²⁹Th via Quantum Interference
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nuclear E2 transition amplitude of ²²⁹Th probes nuclear deformation and configuration mixing, yet remains poorly constrained by measurements dominated by M1 radiation. We propose to determine its magnitude and sign relative to the nuclear M1 transition amplitude through quantum interference in ²²⁹Th³⁺. Two coherent laser fields couple a superposition of initial hyperfine states to a common nuclear isomeric state through the electronic shell. Varying the mixing angle controls interference between the excitation pathways, allowing the signed E2/M1 transition amplitude ratio to be extracted using the calibrated laser-field amplitude ratio, without absolute intensity calibration. An independent M1 reference then determines the E2 magnitude. Dynamical calculations support the feasibility of the scheme, predicting appreciable nuclear excitation with milliwatt laser power on millisecond timescales. We evaluate the extraction sensitivity to experimental and atomic-structure uncertainties. The approach extends to other ²²⁹Th ions, whose rich level structures offer a broader selection of transitions and promising routes to suppress systematic uncertainties.

articles.title: Reactive Phase Change of a Single Droplet in Turbulent Flow with Reactive Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium Using a Two-Scalar Diffusive-Interface Method
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reactive phase change fluids have been shown to enhance thermodynamic performance by integrating chemical reactions with thermodynamic cycles. This study investigates the turbulent evaporation of a single droplet using Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) to model the behavior of reactive phase change fluids. Applying Reactive Vapor--Liquid Equilibrium (RVLE) thermodynamics, the study simultaneously captures the dynamics of reactive phase transitions, mass transfer, and heat transfer during the evaporation of dinitrogen tetroxide (N___O___). A second-order phase field framework is used to derive two scalar transport equations, accurately describing species behavior at equilibrium. The equilibrium is maintained by balancing concentration exchange rates across both the liquid-to-vapor and vapor-to-liquid phases. Results indicate that chemical reactivity significantly influences phase transition dynamics, altering the phase dome structure by modifying critical points and the thermodynamic saturation lines. Endothermic and exothermic behaviors are observed at the interface during the fast reversible evaporation process of N___O__₍ₗ₎ ___ 2NO__₍ᵥ,ₗ₎. Turbulence simulations further show enhanced mixing efficiency and improved gas-liquid separation, driven by chaotic flow patterns. This study elucidates the role of reactive phase change fluids in contrast to conventional non-reactive phase flows, emphasizing the influence of chemical reactions on phase transition dynamics and overall system performance..

articles.title: Electronically Rather Than Geometrically Driven Concerted Proton Transfer under Graphene Confinement
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proton transfer in water is a common yet mechanistically non-trivial phenomenon that underpins proton conduction and chemical reactivity. However, how confinement alters it, and whether the changes are driven by geometry or by electronic interaction, remains far from fully understood. Here, using a water hexamer confined between two graphene sheets as a model system, we combine coupled-cluster and first-principles calculations with energy decomposition to investigate how confinement alters its concerted proton transfer. We find that tightening the confinement lowers the electronic proton-transfer barrier. This reduction does not arise from the geometric distortion of the ring, which merely accompanies the confinement, but from the orbital stabilization of the transition state by the graphene walls. These results demonstrate that the proton-transfer barrier under confinement is governed by electronic rather than geometric factors, providing a mechanistic design principle for tailoring proton conduction and chemical reactivity through nanoscale confinement.

articles.title: Nonideal Absorbers in Hot-Carrier and Hot-Absorber Solar Cells: Losses and Heat Recycling
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The hot carrier solar cell exhibits a photovoltaic conversion efficiency limit of 85.4%. Among the idealizations necessary to achieve this efficiency, it has traditionally been considered essential that the electrons absorbing sunlight do not end up transferring the captured energy to the crystal lattice. In this work, we argue that such a requirement is not necessary if the absorber is thermally insulated. In our analysis, we also consider the possibility of ohmic losses in the absorber due to finite electrical conductivity. We also demonstrate that such losses, delivered as heat, can be partially recycled into electrical work with an efficiency that is given by the Carnot factor. The high efficiencies reported here are thermodynamic limits obtained with ideal energy-selective contacts and negligible parasitic contact conductance, not projections of practical device efficiency. Our work includes a sensitivity analysis for finite contact-mediated heat leakage, and the results are presented as design targets.

articles.title: Semiclassical Quantum Mechanics and the Optics of Time-Varying Media
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid, high contrast modulation of optical parameters such as the refractive index can radically reshape a wave's frequency spectrum as it propagates. Non-commuting frequency and time operators can be used to describe this reshaping, analogous to the position and momentum operators of quantum mechanics. Here we develop the connection between this theory and semi-classical quantum mechanics, showing that: (i) different microscopic models of time-varying materials are equivalent to choices of operator ordering; (ii) wave propagation is governed by an unusual non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation; (iii) we can take a semi-classical limit, finding a generalization of Hamilton's equations governing the central frequency and arrival time of a wave spectrum as it propagates through a modulated material. The theory can be applied to design dispersive time modulations that `focus' a wave in frequency and time, analogous to caustics in semiclassical quantum mechanics. Our results not only deepen the connection between classical wave propagation and quantum mechanics, but can also simplify overly complex calculations that have been previously applied to media where time reflection effects are negligible.

articles.title: Moment-Fourier approach to parallel closures and transport for a toroidally confined multi-ion plasma
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a multi-ion closure framework for tokamak plasmas by solving the drift-kinetic equation using the moment-Fourier method. The model extends our previous single-ion formulation to plasmas containing multiple ion species and consistently incorporates inter-species collisional effects in the moment system. As a representative case, we consider a deuterium-carbon plasma, assuming a common zeroth-order ion temperature on each flux surface while allowing the electron temperature to differ. The first-order fluid moments, namely density, temperature, and parallel flow velocity, are computed for electrons, deuterium ions, and carbon ions. The framework enables a direct comparison of the first-order parallel flow velocities of deuterium and carbon ions, thereby providing a quantitative basis for interpreting charge-exchange spectroscopy measurements and for systematic multi-ion neoclassical transport studies.

articles.title: Phase-Controlled Time-Dependent Modal Analysis of Vortex-Gust Interaction with a Cylinder Wake
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A vortex gust interacting with the periodic wake of a circular cylinder at Re=100 is studied using time-dependent dynamic mode decomposition with phase control (tDMDpc). To examine the phase dependence of the wake and lift responses, the same vortex gust is imposed at 64 shedding phases. For these phase-controlled responses, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) with time-independent spatial modes characterizes departures from the periodic wake, whereas tDMDpc resolves evolving structures and the frequency and growth rate of the fundamental mode. In this decomposition, the approaching gust is mainly captured by the zero-frequency mode. During the encounter, however, gust-related structures develop in the fundamental mode and persist near the cylinder as the gust convects downstream. The fundamental-mode coefficient magnitude is nearly uniform across phases at arrival but becomes phase dependent afterward. Consistent with this phase dependence, the near-wake vorticity amplitude of the fundamental conjugate pair decreases at α=π/2 and increases at α=3π/2 relative to the respective pre-encounter values, matching the inward and outward departures of the POD trajectories. To connect these structures to the cylinder lift, modal pressure and viscous stresses are integrated over the cylinder surface. The zero-frequency contribution carries most of the lift variation at arrival, whereas the fundamental conjugate pair dominates later oscillations. Phase averaging cannot separate these contributions because the fundamental oscillations no longer cancel across phases after the encounter. Their separation reveals that opposing contributions can yield nearly zero total lift despite an appreciable fundamental contribution. As the wake recovers, the lift amplitude approaches its undisturbed value, but a phase shift persists.

articles.title: Bound States in the Continuum as Converging Scattering Zeros in Metasurfaces: Why Accidental BICs Require Nonlocality
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) allow metasurfaces to achieve extremely high quality factors, yet it remains unclear how they emerge and how they can be described by effective material parameters. We address this question by modeling BICs through the reflection and transmission zeros of a metasurface described by effective susceptibilities. By decomposing its response into even and odd parts, and inspecting the interaction of the corresponding poles and zeros, we show that a high-Q resonance appears as a transmission zero squeezed between two reflection zeros, or vice versa. The separation between these scattering zeros is set by the linewidth of the corresponding even or odd resonance, so that a BIC corresponds to a convergence of these zeros. This simple concept explains symmetry-protected BICs and their transformation into quasi-BICs. However, it also reveals a fundamental limitation for accidental BICs: in a passive local dipolar model, the zeros cannot converge at oblique incidence unless one of the susceptibility resonances has a negative amplitude, which would make the metasurface active according to Foster's theorem. We demonstrate that this negative amplitude is in fact the signature of higher-order multipoles or lattice coupling effects that the local model cannot properly capture, which shows that accidental BICs are intrinsically nonlocal. We confirm this conclusion by simulating a silicon-ridge metasurface, whose response is reproduced and predicted by a passive, spatially dispersive model, which also describes how breaking the mirror symmetry of the metasurface turns the accidental BIC into a quasi-BIC.

articles.title: Where hurricanes get their spin: angular momentum versus kinetic energy
articles.abstract: arXiv:2611.24476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tropical cyclones almost never form within a few degrees of the equator. Their energy source, the heat engine fueled by the warm ocean, is available there as everywhere else. What is missing must be the other ingredient a cyclone needs, absolute angular momentum about the local vertical. Across reconnaissance intensity categories, characteristic wind energy increases and the radius of maximum wind decreases, while the characteristic specific absolute angular momentum M varies comparatively little; energy and absolute angular momentum are thus supplied separately.
